He said:	Mr. Speaker, I do not know

subtopic: BILLS PROPOSED TO AUTHORIZE THE CONSTRUCTION OF BRANCH LINES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before you leave the chair, there are certain observations that I would like to bring to your attention and to the attention of the House, relevant to the various resolutions now standing in the name of the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham). These resolutions to be brought down by the minister in question contemplate the construction of twenty-six lines of railway aggregating in the neighbourhood of 1,000 miles, and costing approximately or slightly over $28,000,000. It, therefore, seems to me to go without saying that the matter is one of great moment to the country, one that should not be allowed to pass this House without the most careful scrutiny and without our taking into consideration all the facts relating to these proposals which are to be brought before this legislative body.
It is not my intention, in the course of these remarks, to direct any particular motive towards any particular branch line. I desire to discuss the question of branch lines to be brought down in these resolutions in a more or less general manner; but I wish to point out to the House the large amount involved in these undertakings, and also to say that any undertaking which is not absolutely essential for the welfare of the country generally, or actually and vitally necessary for any particular part of our population, should certainly in every respect be eliminated. The government should have in mind in proposing these various resolutions one consideration only, namely, the vital necessity to the country of any expenditures involved, before a single dollar is expended' on these undertakings. As I have stated, these proposals entail an expenditure of $28,000,000, and for any of us in this House to say that we can spend twenty-eight million dollars, or even twenty-eight million cents, with a free hand in view of the condition of our finances

at the present time is the height of absurdity. As a matter of fact, unless we get down to the lowest possible expenditure in Canada it will be utterly impossible for us to reduce the taxation which is so heavily weighing upon the people to-day; and unless that taxation is reduced to a very considerable extent it will also be impossible for any business, whether it be agricultural or otherwise, to succeed in the future. I think, Sir, that we ought to realize what an exceedingly difficult position we are in to-day in Canada. We are living beside the richest, one of the most populous, and one of the most progressive people in the wide world. In some respect in this country we are not free agents. As regards the question of wages and salaries, and in relation to other matters of that kind, we are controlled, not by our own desires but by the rates of wages and salaries that obtain in the United States; we are governed very largely by what the nation to the south of us may do in these directions. In other words, what the richest nation in the world may do we in Canada are bound also to do, so far as wages and other questions of that kind are concerned.
We have also to take into consideration this fact., that if direct taxation in the United States is lower than direct taxation in this country, then it simply means that our population will drift to the south. Some weeks ago, speaking in the House on other subjects, I directed the attention of the government to the exodus which was then taking place and which had been going on for a number of years. I do not think that we can say at this moment that that exodus has entirely ceased; in fact, I believe it is still in progress. And I do not think that the government or ourselves should be lulled into any false sense of security, or into any ungrounded satisfaction, in the suggestion that those people who leave Canada to go to the United States will surely return; because there is not the slightest shadow of doubt that many of our people, and some of the very best of them, who go to the United States never return but stay there. I say therefore that any expenditure, which the government considers necessary, should be made only from the standpoint of urgent and vital necessity; and such expenditure must be brought down to the very lowest possible figure, either if we expect to have our taxation on a par with the taxation that is levied in the United States- and I am speaking just now of direct taxation -or if we desire to retain our population. It

C. N. R.-Branch Lines
goes without saying, of course, that if taxation in the United States is lower than taxation here, most inevitably the drift of the population must continue to the southern country. Now, I do not wish it to be understood that I am saying in this House that we should not undertake any capital expenditures at all;
I believe that in a new country which is progressing as we are, and in a more or less constructive period, it would be exceedingly stupid for any man to say that we should refrain from capital expenditures. On the other hand, if we do decide upon capital expenditure of any description, as for instance in connection with these branch lines, we should look forward very carefully to make sure that that capital expenditure will be productive of a commensurate advantage. We must not act merely upon conjecture; we must be quite certain that it will be worth while and that it will serve some vital need of the people before we vote any such expenditure. So that, with all due respect to my hon. friends on this side of the House, and without the slightest desire to court unpopularity, I say, in the most decided and distinct terms, that I will support these various resolutions only in so far as I am convinced by the most ample explanations and the most adequate information on the part of the minister that the lines are necessary and that the money expended on them is essential in every particular in order to serve a vital need without which we cannot do. I wish to make myself abundantly clear in that respect, so that in the course of the various resolutions and the subsequent bills which may come up, if any information is asked for, the government and the minister in particular will know precisely the stand I take in this House and before the country in reference to this matter.
I do not think that we in this House and in the country as a whole can shut our eyes to the actual railway situation as it now exists. I offer no comment at all on the question as to how that railway situation was brought about, for I do not think that we are particular!}' concerned at the moment as to how it all happened. We are however vitally con-erned with what is actually happening and what may happen in the future. This we must take into consideration at every step; but I doubt very much whether the nation at large or, if I may say so, every hon. member in this House, quite realizes the vast amount of money which we have expended on these undertakings. Possibly many people think that when the estimates are brought down, or when an operating deficit or a profit, as the case may be, is indicated, there is no need any
longer to worry about the railways. They do not realize that in the ordinary debt of the country there is a huge burden, an indebtedness on which we are paying interest all the time, and in relation to the railways themselves; because the indebtedness in that respect is part of our national debt. In other words, we cannot build or buy railways and think that the money will simply be segregated in a certain account and that we shall not have to pay any interest on it. Money has to come from somewhere, and if it does the cost of it has actually to be paid in one account or another. We have expended vast sums in these railways; there are vast sums locked up in the public accounts and in various other accounts; and there are a number of accounts which I think it will interest hon. members and the country as well to know. I think the people would like to know just what is the liability of the Dominion of Canada in connection with our railways. I do not like wearying the House, and it is with great reluctance that I venture to read statements of figures and accounts. But there is no other method open to me of getting these figures on Hansard, and as I think they are of sufficient importance to hon. members and to the country at large I shall ask the indulgence of the House while I submit them. First of all, there is the actual cash which has been invested in these various lines. That cash invested in these lines, as at December 31, 1923, amounted to the vast sum of $1,138,600,430.

Yes, they are now operated as the Canadian National Railways system. I will give my hon. friend the division of that particular amount in a moment. It may interest him to have this information. First I will give the main headings. We have expended on these railways, by way of so-called advances, large sums of money on which the interest has not entirely been paid. Then come certain securities which the Dominion guaranteed, the interest on which has to be paid, and eventually the principal also. Then there is a class of securities, so-called guaranteed as to interest only. I think that is a misnomer, for as a matter of fact if interest be guaranteed the capital also is guaranteed, because the obligation to pay interest cannot be of any value unless the capital is eventually paid off. So it virtually means that both capital and interest on those securities are guaranteed by the Dominion After those again we have a mass of so-

called unguaranteed securities. In those are included many millions of underlying liens, some guaranteed by various provinces, others not guaranteed at all, but all secured on the various roads of the system forming part of the National lines at the present time, and although not actually assumed-using the word in its very strictest sense-nevertheless they are virtually assumed by the Dominion, as owners of the property for the reason that if any particular block of securities became due and the interest was not paid, it would simply mean that a certain section of the line would be taken by the bond holders. Therefore as a matter of fact we have assumed those securities also, though they are not directly guaranteed.

Now, this is a very pretty bill, Mr. Speaker, on which we have to pay interest. We can do it. speechtext: As to the income convertibles, I am not prepared to answer my right hon. friend at the moment. I could do so if I delayed to look up the figures here, but I presume the matter is not of sufficient importance at the moment for me to do so. Now, Mr. Speaker, the government is asking for a vote of $56,000,000 for the ordinary railway loans. In that sum there is, not included, of course, this additional $28,000,000. Last year we were asked for something like $74,550,000, or about $18,000,000 more than this year. This represents the gain in operating earnings of the Canadian National Railways, and possibly it may be said that in view of this gain we are justified in branching out and spending more money on our railway system, but I do not think there is any justification for this view. It would seem to me very absurd and most unreasonable that after spending something like $390,000,000 on these roads during the last three years alone there should not have been a very distinct improvement in the railway earnings, and for that reason I do not think we should be exuberant in praise or too generous in our attitude with regard to the

spending of money on the building of branch lines, except, as I have stated, where they are absolutely essential.
In these operating deficits or in the operating surpluses, as the case may be, the actual interest payable to the government of Canada is not included or taken into consideration, to say nothing about the interest on the capital amounts which has been paid and which has been placed in the system. These fixed charges are continuing and are increasing materially every year. For example, in 1920 the fixed charges due the Dominion were $13,000,000. In 1921 they had increased to $19,000,000; in 1922 they were $24,000,000 and in 1923 they were $29,000,000. In other words, the amount of money payable on loans made and on indebtedness to the Dominion of Canada, not including operating deficits or earnings, was $29,000,000 on the 31st of December last.
There is another point that I think we should take into consideration: we are wont in this House to say, "Let us keep the railways out of politics;" or, "The board of directors say we should do this or should do that." I do not think we can hide behind statements of that kind. We have to accept our own responsibility in this House for the money we spend on branch lines or on any other part of the railway system. So far as I am concerned, I am not going to hide behind the cry that the railways should be kept out of politics or that the board of directors say this or say that. I want to know myself what the expenditure is to be before I share any responsibility in the matter.
In addition to that, we shall probably be told that the budget will balance this year. I am not uttering criticisms, Mr. Speaker, in this respect; I am simply stating cold facts. Twenty-eight millions is a huge sum of money and should not, either in whole or in part, be voted in this House until we know precisely what we are doing. It may be argued that on account of the budget being balanced we should branch out still more, but in my opinion that is no reason at all. I am glad to know that the budget is likely to balance, but if it does it will be because we have too great war taxes on the country, the surpluses from which are being used for other purposes, not war at all. If there is a surplus of war taxes-and I know there is -then those war taxes should be remitted, cancelled or reduced.
We are very likely to be told as regards these branch lines that in view of the reduction in the estimates we should proceed with

8&8

the proposed construction. I know there has been a very considerable reduction in the estimates and I commend the government for it. That reduction, exclusive of railway expenditure, amounts to 127,000,000, of which probably $10,000,000 is due to the slackening off of war services. In other words it is due to the fact that those war services have slackened off in the ordinary course of events and have not been specially diminished in any way-services which are paid, Mr. Speaker, with war taxes. That means that there is a reduction in the estimates this year of $17,000,000, and that reduction will be not as great when the supplementaries come down. Therefore I submit that the fact that there is a reduction in the estimates is no reason at all why we should build branch lines and more railways.
These resolutions are brought down at this time of the session, and before the budget, no doubt for certain very good reasons. They are brought down, I suppose, at this particular season of the year in order that the engineers may get to work on their estimates, get their plant on the ground and start the construction, in accordance with any vote passed by this House and by the other House, in ample time during the coming summer. That is sense, there is no doubt about that; it is a good season for the measures being brought down at this time. But notwithstanding that, it seems to me that we are entitled to know exactly how our budget is going to stand for the next year before we vote $28,000,000. Business at present is not satisfied, particularly in view of the heavy taxes that are being paid. Many say that business is prosperous, but I am of the opinion that it is not as prosperous as many seem to think. Business wants to know how we are going to stand for the next fiscal year before undertaking a measure of this kind.
It was indicated by certain proposals of the government that there might be changes in the tariff, and cities in particular have been very much disturbed as to what those changes might be. I do not know what the actual proposals are; nobody knows what they are; but business is very distinctly disturbed in that connection, and I venture to say that if proposals are brought down which will injure business interests or will not improve business interests, -which without doubt need improvement at the present time, certain parts of this country will not agree to the building of any of these lines. We want to know before expending money exactly where we stand, and I think we are entitled to

know before voting this large sum precisely what is the fiscal policy of the government.
Without discussing any particular branch lines, I wish to say that I have taken the opportunity^ of studying, by the 4 p.m. map and by such information as I have been able to procure, the various lines which are projected. Some of these lines, it is alleged, should be built because certain grading has already been done. It is urged, not by the minister but by others, that for this reason we should put rails on these gradings and complete them into railways. But in my opinion the fact that these gradings exist is no reason whatever for taking that course. If we have spent money on the grading of these lines and if it has been unwise to proceed further, the mere fact-I repeat, the mere fact; I do not want hon. members to misunderstand me- that these lines are graded and that money has been spent op the grading is no reason why millions more should be spent in turning them into profitless branch line railways.
In addition to that, so far as I can see, pome of these lines are too near other existing lines and therefore are not essential. In other cases there is too little population to serve and there is not likely to be any additional population in these particular localities for some considerable time. In other cases I believe traffic arrangements could be made with other railway companies which would obviate the building of additional lines. In other cases I can find no reason whatever why the projected lines should be built, and I doubt if any railway engineer could find any. In that connection, Sir, I may point out that we have millions of acres near railways which we can use without spending enormous sums for the building of lines into sparsely populated territory.
In conclusion, as regards the remarks which I have been making I want to say this-and it has reference to a fact which, I think, is not fully understood or fully grasped-we have in this country at present two great railway systems, the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific.
I think every member of this House, I think everybody in this country, should wish well for both these lines, they are both great national undertakings. But to say that the Canadian National system should progress because of unfair competition with the Canadian Pacific line is senseless in the extreme. The Canadian Pacific is just as great a national asset as the Canadian National line. In addition to that, the Canadian Pacific is known

C.N.R.-Branch Lines
all over the world by reason of its stability in management and in finance and is, as a matter of fact, all hon. members will admit, a source of pride to this country. The Canadian Pacific is financed by its own efforts on its own credit and on its own ability, whereas all the Canadian National railway line has to do is to to come to this House and get money, and it usually gets the money it requires. Now, to have competition between these two lines is senseless in the extreme. If traffic arrangements can be made with one line to help out another line, I think those arrangements should be made. To build lines unnecessarily when there is not enough traffic to satisfy both these systems is not putting this House, is not putting this country, in a position to get lower freight rates in the very slightest degree. What we need in this country and what we must all try to get is lower transportation costs. That is what we want. Building branch railway lines may yield pleasure but that is not going to give us lower transportation costs if other railway lines are there to serve the particular purpose which the proposed new lines are intended to serve. I wish to make that point abundantly and absolutely clear in every respect, and I particularly wish to repeat- that where it is possible to make traffic arrangements with another railway these branch lines, as suggested, should not be constructed simply for the purpose of building them. In addition there is a great deal of duplication of services in this country between these two railways. I believe traffic arrangements could be made between the two systems that would be most satisfactory. Why should not such traffic arrangements be made, why should not such duplication be avoided? Why should not such duplication be remedied with a view to bringing the operating costs of both systems down to a minimum and making their operating and general profits greater?

so that in course of time we shall be prepared to demand lower transportation costs. That is what we must have in mind in connection with these proposals brought down by the minister. The object should be not to build further railways, not to spend money unnecessarily, but to get lower transportation costs and see that both these great railway companies shall survive and prosper.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I will take my seat merely adding these few words. When these bills are brought down I shall expect the fullest information from the minister- and and this no doubt he will give in his usual admirable manner. I shall want to know how the expenditures are to be met and what
reasons there are for building these different branch lines before I will support the proposals.

Has the hon. member
taken into consideration the St. Lawrence river improvements upon which this country is expending millions of dollars a year?

I am quite ready
to admit that my hon. friend's argument has its
C.N.R.-Branch Lines

value but at present Lam dealing with railways. Now this resolution and the bill which will follow proposes that 965 miles of railway should be built at an expenditure of $28,311,300. Out of the 965 miles now being proposed Quebec will have 31 miles, with an expenditure of $1,462,000.
Is the hon. gentleman aware of the benefits the province of Quebec receives through its shipping ports from the extra branch lines and railroads in the western provinces?

I am aware of all that, but this is another question altogether. I could not answer offhand a question like that. If I were to answer the question of my hon. friend I should have to go into details as to the cost of the railways and the improvements made in the St. Lawrence, and so forth, and this is a matter which is outside of the question I have been discussing. I shall be quite willing to hear my hon. friend discuss the question as to why further railways should be built in the West.
It would be very much better if my hon. friend had made a comparison of the railways constructed in the West as compared with those constructed in Quebec.

Has the hon. membei taken into consideration the fact that in Quebec last year there was expended for transportation	'purposes-harbours,	rivers
and so forth-the sum of $1,137,650.50, as against an expenditure in Saskatchewan and Alberta of $34,000?
Yes, I take that into consideration, and if you take into consideration the fact that the province of Quebec is paying for the railroads of the West-
Oh, oh.

This is a fact
which will be proven on investigation, and there is no question about it. In answer to my hon. friend I say that this million and a half is just one drop in the bucket compared to what we are paying for railroads in the West. We have deficits of hundreds of millions of dollars on these railways that have

C.N.R.-Branch Lines
been built where they should not have been built.
Now let us make another comparison. In the United States they have one mile of railway for every four hundred inhabitants, in Canada we have one mile of railway for every two hundred inhabitants; and in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia they have one mile of railway for every one hundred inhabitants. These lines by the very nature of things must come out of the moneys of the country, and must increase the deficits, and the province of Quebec is paying for this.

Is the hon. gentleman
not aware that the western lines produce the paying tonnage and the eastern lines do not?

I will be ready
to listen to my hon. friend when he undertakes to prove that the western lines are paying for themselves. My knowledge is that they do not pay for themselves, and until the proof is furnished I maintain they do not. He advances the proposition that they are the railways that pay. It will be for him to prove that, but that is another argument altogether. I was answering my hon. friend when he stated that there was expended in Quebec for wharves and harbours and improvements of the St. Lawrence, one million and a half last year. This is an insignificant sum compared to what these railways are costing us.

We pay that every
year.

But the railways are piling up an enormous defiicit every year. Coming back to my subject more definitely, I say there are in the province of Quebec many localities where railways are just as badly needed as they are in the West. I will give you one example. I do not want to be parochial, but I would refer to Joliette and Berthier which are my county and the adjoining county where there are communities with populations of 7,000, and they are sixty miles from a railway. Those communities have been in existence for over thirty years, and there is a great deal of traffic through that part of the country. If a railway were built there, it could develop that traffic and the country could develop, but the country cannot at present develop because it is too far ffom a railway. When requests are made for railways, the answer comes necessarily:	"We have no money to
build them." I am ready to admit that money is scarce; but we cannot on the one hand
say that there is no money to build a railway in Quebec, and on the other say that there is money to build railways in the West.
I have every consideration for my hon. friends from the West and the other provinces, but I have shown now that Quebec is very far behind any of the other provinces of this Dominion as regards the building of railways.
What is this confederation? It is an agglomeration of nine provinces, in which the* interests, in many instances, are absolutely different, if not opposed one to another. What means has a province to advance its own interests? Its influence, and the influence in this case comes through the population. The province that is most populous is most important in this confederation-I mean in point of activity and influence-by the very nature of things. The province that has the least population has the least influence. It is reasonable for any citizen of any province to claim that his province should have the railways which it deserves, because railways bring population and population means importance and influence in this Dominion. For all these reasons, while I am not prepared to say that I shall be opposed to every one of these resolutions, 1 want to reserve my right to examine each and every one of them, and I feel convinced, unless I should change my opinion in the meantime-and that is not likely-that the greater part of these resolutions =hould be discarded.

Mr. Speaker, I intend to say only a few words, because I am aware that on this side of the House there may be members who are able to speak with better knowledge than I regarding some of these branch lines. I want, however, to reply to some of the remarks made by the two previous speakers. I think it goes without saying that in this House we are all standing for economy, only our ideas as to what economy means may differ a little, sometimes on account of the particular point of view from which we view the question of economy.
Oh, oh.

If hon, gentlemen to my right will wait until I begin to express my views, perhaps they will know what I intend to speak about. It is rather surprising to find so much interest taken, before one begins to speak, as regards what one is going to say.
We hear continually about the drift of population to the south and the causes of that drift of people from Canada to the
C.N.R.-Branch Lines

United States. I think I mentioned before that there will always be a certain number drifting over the line to the large population to the south of us. At the same time, I think we will all admit that present circumstances with us are not such as they might be to conduce to keep our people at home. I am willing to admit that hon. members in all parts of this House are quite as sincere as I am in their endeavours to better conditions, and to see that this Canada of ours shall be as prosperous as it can possibly be made.
I have no intention to discuss this matter ifrom the standpoint of any particular province. .1 realise, as the last speaker has said, that there are difficulties in governing this country owing to its geographical and physical conditions. I believe all of u? ought to consider from a national point of view the various items that come before us for our consideration. It is quite human that most of us will be influenced by the locality from which we come and the environment by which we are surrounded in that locality; but I think it is possible to divest ourselves of that state of feeling and to judge things with some degree of fairness to all parties concerned.
As regards the branch lines in the West,
I think Manitoba has only one small branch line. Quite a number, however, of branch lines are in the western prairie provinces. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George- (Mr. Marler) was very particular to inform the House that he was not going to support any of those lines unless they were absolutely needed.

I was referring to no
particular lines in any province whatsoever.

I quite agree with that. I
was rather unfortunate in the way I made the remark. I meant all branch lines.

I did not say that I would not support any particular branch line. I stated that no branch line should be built except where necessary and essential. I think my hon. friend will very likely agree with me in that.

My hon. friend has put the
matter better than I could put it. That was exactly what I was going to say. I quite agree with the hon. member, and I will support no line unless it is absolutely necessary and a paying proposition to build. That is the position which I would take as regards any line that is proposed at the present time. I will say a few words about that later on. ,
The statement was made that we must keep our railways out of politics. I could not

help thinking that the hon. member was putting up a straw man simply to knock him down, because we all know that when the question is one of voting money for the Canadian National Railways, that question must come before this parliament, so when we speak about keeping the National Railways out of politics, we do not mean it in that way. If money is required for capital expenditure on the Canadian National Railways, it will have to be voted by this parliament.
Another remark was made regarding business, and I paid particular attention to that remark, because it was bracketed with the tariff. It seems to me that no address can be made in this House unless the tariff appears in it. The hon. member referred to the fact that there were certain rumours in regard to the tariff. I cannot quote his exact words, but I think I caught the meaning that business was so alarmed, in such a precarious position, that it would be very difficult to get money to build branch lines as long as business was in that particular frame of mind.
I think I have the idea fairly that if business were put into a safe position through the tariff being stable, or put into the position that business would want, possibly we could go on and build branch lines. I do not know whether I drew the inference correctly, but that is the inference which I draw from the remarks ffiade at that particular time.

There was no suggestion
on my part that money could not be obtained to build branch lines having respect to the tariff. What I intended to convey was this, that business was not at the present time certain what the tariff proposals of the government might be, and I thought it better that the fiscal policy should be definitely known before we expended a large amount of money on branch lines or anything else.

I accept the hon. member's
statement. It is pretty much along the line of what I tried to convey myself. He probably has a better command of language and 1 can put the question more clearly than I can. As regards the situation in business,
I am quite in sympathy with having industry prosper and I wish to see it prosper. When the question of taxation is referred to it is always spoken of as being something that presses heavily upon business. Well, let me say that taxation presses heavily upon all the people.	,

That is precisely what I said in my opening remarks; I pointed out that taxation pressed heavily upon both agriculture and business.

C.N.R.-Branch Lines

That being the case, I do not see why I should be making this speech, because the hon. member has already apparently stated everything that I have to say. He also made reference to the rivalry between the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National Railways. No one in this House harbours any antipathy at all to the Canadian Pacific Railway or regards it in an attitude of antagonism. It is one of the greatest institutions the world has ever known, and we as Canadians are proud of the fact that we have the Canadian Pacific Railway in this country. So that we can, I think, dismiss from our minds any idea of hostility to that great corporation. At the same time, however, we want to look after our own interests as far as we can just as the Canadian Pacific Railway Company are doing from their own point of view. With the Canadian National Railways the position is somewhat different. We are interested not only in the efficient operation of the roads but, as well, in the financial success of the whole concern, because the success of these railways is a matter that affects not only our national pride but our national pocket as well, and we must see to it that they are made prosperous. I do not like to speak in a particularly optimistic tone in regard to the future of the railways, but I believe that at no very distant time hence a great many of our difficulties in connection with the Canadian National system will disappear with a growing population and growing business, and that the great burden that at present weighs down upon us will have been partly lifted from our shoulders.
A remark was made by an hon. member regarding the mileage of railways that were being built in the different provinces. I do not know that this is the happiest way of approaching the consideration of this subject. I think that the needs of the various provinces would constitute a better basis upon which to discuss the matter. Population per mile is not, in my opinion, a satisfactory standpoint from which to examine the railway situation in any province; rather, I think that the earning power per capita of the population for producing traffic for the railways would be a much fairer way of arriving at the true mileage which the, people in any particular locality should have. On this basis I claim that in the three prairie provinces the people produce more tonnage per mile than is produced in any other province in the Dominion. I dislike mentioning personal affairs, but if I may be pardoned I may say that I have shipped as many as thirteen and
fourteen cars of wheat in one year, which is a very large amount of tonnage for one individual to produce. This of course may not be typical of the entire prairie country, but I consider that the population of these provinces produces a larger tonnage of freight for the railways than any other province in Canada.
Or any other place in the world.

It is a well known fact that the paying mileage of the railways is in the West. Hon. members from the East are continually asserting the fact that the great burden of the railways is put upon the shoulders of the people, and that the country is building western lines.
Not everyone says that.

Well, a good many people do. But they seem to forget that had the railway mileage stopped at Fort William, there would never have been such large dividends as ha,ve been earned by the prairie lines that were constructed from Fort William, west. Never in the history of railways have larger dividends been paid than on the western lines, but these dividends would not have been possible had the mileage stopped at Fort William. I have no hostility to the province of Quebec; indeed, I like that province and its people. But I want them to bear in mind the fact I have just stated. I do not like to see any question discussed in this House purely from a provincial point of view. It is absolutely necessary, of course, when members of parliament come here to represent certain sections of the country, that they shall look after the interests of those particular localities. But, while this must be done, I hope it will aways be done in the proper spirit and with a view to cultivating that broad national outlook which I am sure we all trust will be characteristic of the Canadian people before long.

I do not propose delaying the House long with the observations that I have to make, but I feel that an expression of gratitude should be tendered the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler), for the very able manner in which he has dealt with this matter. I believe that it is of vital importance, in considering this large number of railway bills that we should have always before us the financial condition of the country. To say whether one was in favour of branch lines or not would be as ridiculous as to say whether a man liked vegetables or not; there
C.N.R.-Branch Lines

would be some which he would like and others which he would not like. I do not think that we can consider these branch lines in a lump; each one will have to be taken up and examined carefully, and, in my opinion, the light in which we should view this question is the light of this principle- that we in this country cannot afford to spend money upon anything except vital necessities.

Oh, oh.
Mr. MeMASTER:	It would be well, I
think, if we could all look at this question in a purely judicial and impartial frame of mind-. The information which I suggest the minister should be prepared to lay before parliament is this: First, what extent of territory will be served by the proposed line: second, what number of persons will be so served; third, how far are such persons distant now from the nearest railway facilities?

Most of them are still in
Europe.
Mr. MeMASTER: Well, I did not intend to give an international aspect to the matter;
I should be content to consider merely the number of people in Canada who are distant from the nearest railway facilities. Then I think we should have some computation, rough though it might be, of the-amount of tonnage that might be carried on the proposed branch lines, as well as the estimated earnings. The estimated profit to be obtained in the immediate, and the more distant future should also be considered. I can well understand that it might be good business to build a line even although for a year or so it might be a liability rather than an asset, if there were a very strong assurance that 
within two or three years that liability would be turned into an asset. I do not wish to detain the House much .longer, but it seems to me that it is in the light of this principle, and with the information which I seek, that we should bring our minds to a consideration of the different branch lines proposed.

Mr. Speaker, I had not intended detaining the House with any remarks at this moment, but I deem it necessary to again make clear the position which we take upon this question. My hon. friend the leader of the group to my left (Mr. Forke) pointed out that everything in connection with railways, capital expenditure and the like, had to come before the House, and my hon. friend from St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler) also pointed out that there was a probability of the budget being balanced. Well, both these gentlemen are to a certain extent right, and yet they are wrong. The real reason why we are having all this discussion to-'day, and no branch lines were built last year, is that the ordinary rule of showing railway capital expenditures as a matter of railway vote year by year was departed from. It is quite easy, of course, to show a favourable balance when you change your method of book-keeping, but I think my hon. friend from St. Lawrence-St. George is quite right in saying that the balance should not be taken too seriously in connection with this matter. He might have gone further and said that with respect to that balance we wilt have to consider the wonderful legislation of last year along with the loans of $50,000,000, and $22,500,000 guaranteed by the government. Of course, it makes all the difference whether you do or do not consider in your balance $72,500,000.
Were those loans considered in previous years?

My hon. friend
will correct me if I am wrong, but I think there was never a loan which was not brought down to this House and duly voted. However that may be, we have got further admissions at the present time from my hon. friend himself, and I care not, and this House cannot-very well distinguish, what he does one way or the other with the money in the light of his own admission that we already have many more millions of dollars invested in this property than it is worth.

A year or so ago my hon. friend stated that we had to spend money on these properties.

C.N.R.-Branch Lines
I fail to see the significance of having had to spend it.

Well, the significance is
here. The money had to be spent, my hon. friend said, because trains were running off the tracks.

Oh yes, my hon. friend is perfectly correct, but he is referring to something that I am not addressing myself to at the moment. It is quite correct to say that in the past money had absolutely to be spent in order to provide a proper vehicle of transportation, and the capital so spent in betterments and reconstruction is to be found in the deficits voted by this House. As I say, Mr. Speaker, the only reason for the delay last year was that a new method might be adopted and the old basis of comparison confused, with the resultant loss of time. There was something said to the effect that the money for these branch lines cannot be got quick enough by vote. Well, sir, we have already voted one-sixth of the estimates without a word of discussion. In connection with these branch lines there is no reason in the world why the estimates could not have been brought down at the very commencement of the session and the votes dealt with. That is not the reason. The reason is that it is thought to be a good thing to get a change of basis.
I do not want to delay consideration of these bills. I think that probably most of the branch lines will not at all measure up to the standard claimed by my hon. friends who have spoken, that on the contrary they will fall very far short of the standard required, for instance, by the leader of the Progressive party. But some of these branch lines I think do measure up to the standard, and we do not want to delay their proper consideration. We do however, want to get the fullest and completest information with respect to all these projects, and surely that is something which the House is entitled to. Last session we had a great deal of difficulty in getting any information at all. I recall correspondence with my hon. friend (Mr. Graham) complaining of lack of information, and it will be remembered that last session we protested against these matters being dealt with without proper information being furnished to the House. Now, I hope that will not again occur. I would ask the minister to bring down not only the information which the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) has already pointed out should be furnished, but also appropriate maps in order that members will know just exactly where this construction is and its relation to other lines,
so that they will be able to appreciate the effect on the railway situation generally. I think we should also have-and I know that my hon. friend can get it if these matters have been properly considered-the regular traffic report from the traffic officers of the company. And over above all that, I think this House has the right to ask from the gentleman to whom we are all looking for the real operation of these lines-Sir Henry Thornton-a declaration that he requires them and believes that their construction is in the public interest. We do not want to have it said later on, as it very likely may be said in view of the location of some of the lines in this list, that the House rendered it absolutely impossible for the National system to make a proper showing. Therefore, we have a right to such a declaration and to be assured that the proposed construction will not constitute an obstacle to the successful operation of the system in future. I would ask my hon. friend to bring down this information.
I would also like it to be understood that while we yield not our position that railway costs should be shown in the railway estimates, and that the whole matter be properly and fully considered when the bills are in committee, we reserve to ourselves the right to discuss any matter of principle which may arise.

Mr. Speaker, I only rise to say that I fully endorse the remarks made by my hon. friend from St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler) regarding the resolution now before the House. He has made such a forceful speech and has so well covered the ground that I will not weary hon. members with further arguments in support of his attitude. Like him I only wish to make my position clear, and I will do so in two words. On another occasion I stated that it was very difficult to convince some of our constituents that the construction of very important and urgent public works must be deferred at the present moment on account of the economy that we have to practise in our public expenditures. If we are to make expenditures in railway construction which are not absolutely necessary and urgent it will be impossible to convince our constituents of the necessity for delay in other works. Therefore I will await the information which the Minister of Railways will undoubtedly bring down when the resolutions come before the Committee of the Whole House for consideration. I am sure that he will be able to convince us that these projected lines are necessary and urgent at this time. If he does not,
C.N.R.-Branch Lines

I am sorry to say that I shall have to vote against the resolution.

speakeroldname: Mr. G. W. KYTE (Cape Breton South and Richmond):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the subject of the construction of railways in this country is always one in which the representatives in the House of Commons take a deep interest. This afternoon we have listened to a discussion led largely by hon. gentlemen residing in the city of Montreal or in districts within close and ready access to it. We do know that for some years in that city a rivalry has existed between the two great national railway systems of Canada. From the point of view of the districts represented by my hon. friends I presume we have not very much fault to find with their attitude. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, Montreal (Mr. Mar-ler) has no constituents who reside very far from railways.
He has constituents who have to pay for them, though.

Well, the whole people of Canada contribute their proportion. When my hon. friend's constituents desire to leave the city and travel to remoter districts they are not obliged to drive by buggy or automobile a very considerable distance in order to get to the nearest railway. The same is true with regard to my hon. friend from Chambly and Vercheres (Mr. Archambault), he not only has two railways in his riding, but he is advocating very strongly and with great eloquence the building of a bridge to connect his constituency with the city of Montreal.
Very necessary indeed.

I quite agree that that bridge is very necessary from the point of view of the interests of my hon. friend's constituents, but he should also concede that necessary railway accommodation should be extended to rural districts.
Never said a word against it.

I myself live in a constituency that has not the railway accommodation that it ought to have and that the importance of that part of the country calls for. The hon. member for Joliette (Mr. Denis) gave a statement in the course of his speech as to the population served by each mile of railway throughout the different provinces.
I shall not recapitulate his figures, but he pointed out that in British Columbia there (Mr. Archambault.]
was a mile of railway for each 102 of the population; in Ontario, a mile for 5 p.m. each 266, and in Quebec, a mile for each 460. In Nova Scotia there is a population of 326 to each mile of railway. In the island of Cape Breton, which ought to be and has always been regarded as a section of Nova Scotia standing by itself, we have one mile of railway to each 600 of the population. In the United States there is a mile of railway to every 400 of the population. So that from the figures quoted by the hon. member for Joliette and from those I have just given it will be seen that in the important section of Nova Scotia from which I come we have a smaller mileage of railway in proportion to the population than in any other part of Canada.
During the last two years that I have occupied a seat in this House I have not pressed unduly the demands of the people of that part of the country in reference to necessary railway accommodation. I regret very much that in this very generous bill of fare as regards the supplying of branch railways for the different provinces, the hon. Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) has not been able to include the construction of a railway line from the town of St. Peters to the city of Sydney and the town of Louis-burg. Nova Scotia is rich in natural resources; I do not think that in any part of Canada there is greater natural wealth than is to be found in that province. In the island of Cape Breton, which I more particularly represent in this House, there is a still larger amount of wealth in natural resources. We have there all the important coal mines of the Maritime provinces. We have there a great steel plant which gives employment to a larger number of men than probably any other industrial concern in Canada. From the town of St. Peters to the city of Sydney is a distance of sixty miles, and along that line there are valuable coal mines, deposits of ore, and settlements, the people of which make a prosperous living in the pursuit of the fisheries. These people are obliged to haul the products of their industry twenty or thirty miles to a railway. Important lumbering resources which are still undeveloped are also to be found in that section. Recently some important mineral deposits were discovered about thirty miles from the railway. A large and wealthy industrial concern in New York spent some $60,000 or $70,000 prospecting this area. They found the mineral deposits were there, but owing to their being such a long distance from a railway the project had to be aban-

C.N.R.-Branch Lines
doned. The company lost the money they had spent on it, and the mine still remains undeveloped. What was done in Ontario when large mineral deposits were found in that northern country? The moment it was known that it was wealthy in respect of mineral resources, a railway was built to tap that section of the country.
By the province.

By the province; it was a
Liberal government that was in office at the time.

If my hon. friend
will permit a question, does he not recall that the Liberal government in power at that time refused to grant the usual subsidy for the building of that road?

Well, I am not sure as to
that; at all events the Liberal government in Ontario built the railway and it has been a great advantage to that country. I do not propose, however, to be drawn away from the particular matter I have in my mind. I cannot emphasize too strongly the importance of constructing the railway line to which I refer, and while I give enthusiastic support to every proposal calculated to improve the conditions of people living in the rural districts and facilitating the transport to market of the products of their industry, I desire equal consideration for every part of the Dominion of Canada.
In the proposals of the Minister of Railways provision is made for one branch railway for the province of New Brunswick, two for Nova Scotia, three for Quebec, two for Manitoba, ten for Saskatchewan, five for Alberta, and three for British Columbia, making twenty-six branches in all. It was argued by the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. Denis) that owing to the sparse population in these provinces there was no justification for constructing these branch lines of railway. Mr. Speaker, one of the chief justifications for such expenditure is that the building of these railways will increase the population, and will bring more people into the country to assist in developing our resources. What is the situation that exists to-day? It is that population is moving from the rural districts to the urban centres. It is stated from time to time, unfortunately with great truth, that we have to a very large degree lost population from the rural sections. Large numbers of our people, it is alleged, have gone to the United States, and many others have moved from the rural sections to our cities. Why have they done that? Because the conditions of life in the
country are not as favourable or as pleasant as they are in the cities. How can we expect the people to take up farms in sections thirty and forty miles from a railway, how can we expect them to engage in farming and help to develop our natural resources, if there are no railway facilities in the rural sections by which their products can be transported to market. The conditions that exist in western Canada are not peculiar to that part of the country; the conditions existing in the older settled portions of the Maritime provinces call just as loudly for the provision of railway accommodation as do those in the West. It is probably too late now to ask the Minister of Railways to include in his rather comprehensive scheme for the building of branch lines the railway that I have in mind, but I trust that when the House is called upon to consider railway construction at a future session the importance of the line whose construction I advocate will not be overlooked.

Is my hon.

One of the railroad proposals included in the branch line measures presented to parliament last spring and defeated by the Senate, called for construction of a road from a point in New Brunswick to a point on the Maine border, there to establish a connection between the C.N.R. and American railroads. If the proposal, in the same or some other form, comes before parliament during the coming session, it should arouse vigorous St. John opposition. If there were no other reasons for opposition to this measure, it should be sufficient to say that the need for economy makes expenditure of the millions involved an impossibility of the present. But there are other reasons for opposing this railroad construction. The province is already so well gridironed that further railroad construction, except such as is necessary to link up the Canadian National with the Valley road' and provide a direct connection with the port terminals, can be left until development justifies their needs. The Dominion government railroad system has connections through St. John and through northern New Brunswick with railroad systems in the United States. To build another line and cut out the traffic that comes through St. John would entail an enormous expenditure without compensating benefits. In its own interests and in the interests of those economies which all recognize as 
obligatory at this time, St. John should study carefully any railroad proposals so menacing as the construction of another line to the international boundary.

Something more than two millions of the twenty-eight millions of dollars which the Minister of Railways plans to spend on twenty-six branch line railways are for the construction of a road in New Brunswick from Kingsclear, a few miles above Fredericton, to a point on the St. Croix river opposite Vanceboro. A glance at a railway map of New Brunswick will show how this line will sidetrack St. John. At Kingsclear the branch will run from the St. John and Quebec Railway to the international border, forty-two miles away, there to link up with the Maine Central. The purpose of a connection between the Maine Central at Vanceboro and the Quebec and St. John at Kingsclear is to give the Canadian National a more direct American connection than the present St. John and Bangor route. From Kingsclear it is a shorter and more direct run via the National Transcontinental and the Central across country to Moncton and the North Shore than via St. John. The forty-two miles of railway therefore aims to divert from St. John all the east and westbound traffic which now finds its way through this city en route to and from United States points. It will lessen through traffic on the Canadian National Moncton-St. John line. It will lessen through traffic on the Canadian Pacific St. John-Vanceboro line. It will cut both railroad and terminal workers out of much employment without serving any particular traffic necessity. It is the Harvey-Salisbury Railway proposition in an amended form. St. John vigorously opposed that proposition in the long ago, and St. John should vigorously oppose this new effort to sidetrack this city and port by a large public expenditure, unnecessary at any time and absolutely indefensible at this time.
There is one further observation I wish to make at this moment, and that is that there is a good deal to show that the road that is proposed to be built is a competitive road to the Canadian Pacific. I am not advocating the Canadian Pacific interests, nor am I interested in any way in doing so, but I take it that it is the opinion of the House that at the present time our wishes and our views should be that each railroad should now be allowed to carry on its business, and that it is unnecessary and it is extravagant to build further lines of one system-that is to say of the Canadian National system- so that it may compete with the Canadian Pacific; in other words it is not an essential at the present moment.

speechtext:
This branch line is viewed in New Brunswick, or, at least, in that portion over which the Canadian National Railways dominates the traffic, as a business proposition, and it is from that point alone that I wish to approach this subject to-night. If you will look at the map of New Brunswick and visualise the traffic there, you will observe that the Canadian Pacific Railway holds sway in a comparatively small portion of the province, namely in the southeastern corner and along _the western boundary, and that the balance of the country for the most part is served entirely by Canadian National lines. Ever since the mileage of the Intercolonial was increased by the absorption of the Canada Eastern railway, by the building of the St. John and Quebec railway, and by the absorption of the branch lines of the Intercolonial railway in New Brunswick, that system has gathered in each and every year a very considerable quantity of traffic which has been destined for New England points. During all this period of time, that system has been obliged to hand over the traffic thus originating on its lines, either to the Canadian Pacific railway at the city of St. John, or at the city of Fredericton or at Woodstock in the county of Carleton, or to the Bangor and Aroostook railway at Van Buren, Maine. As long ago as 1912, Mr. F. P. Gutelius, then general manager of the Canadian Government Railways-and I ven-IMr. Graham.]
ture to say he is the best man who ever handled the Canadian Government Railways, at least, in my part of the country-conceived the idea of this independent outlet to the New England states for traffic originating on his own lines. I have no doubt, had the war not come, and had Mr. Gutelius continued as general manager of those railways, this independent funnel, so to speak, would have been built long ago.
Let me say, in passing, that as regards the constituency which I have the honour to represent in this House, this question is not a local transportation question at all. It will serve little or no local purpose, and in any event I do not wish to approach the question from that standpoint. I do not, however, believe even the best friend of the project will claim for it that it is for the purpose of serving local traffic conditions. I must confess to the opponents of this project that, viewed from that standpoint, the proposition has no merit; but I say with all sincerity -and I do not care what government brings it forward-that from the standpoint of the management of the Canadian National Railways, this is a business proposition, and while this may not be the time to build it-and about this I can well understand there may be a great diversity of opinion, and I have no quarrel with anybody who takes the view that this is not an opportune time to build it- yet I say that if you were in the position of the management of the Canadian National Railways at this or at any time during the past ten years and had to see your traffic originating on your lines handed over to your keenest competitor in that whole territory, you would sympathise with them in their desire to have an independent outlet for this traffic which has been carried on for more than fifty years into the New England states. I am personally going to ask the committee, aside altogether from the two considerations which I have mentioned, namely the question of local conditions and the question of economic conditions, to view this matter on its merits alone. I believe, if the question is studied, if due regard is given to the problems that confront the management-and I sympathise with them as regards the problems with which I know they have been confronted in the past- this project will receive at least sympathetic consideration at the hands of this House.
I wish we had more information from the minister. I wish the management of the Canadian National Railways had taken us into their confidence and told us the extent of that traffic. I know it is large; I know it must be very large at certain seasons of the

C.N.R.-Branch Lines
year, and I know there has been trouble for years in connection with the traffic to and from New England lines on account of the question of empties which was referred to this afternoon by the minister. At times, there are embargoes on Canadian cars leaving this country from Canadian railways, and it is possible to make shipments, especially of our forest and agricultural products, only in American cars. We have no direct contact with the Boston and Maine system which comprises the Maine Central system as well. Those cars are shipped down to the management of the Canadian National Railways as empties and they are grabbed up by their competitors, with the result that forest products and agricultural products in great volume cannot be moved because of the competitor having taken those empties which were destined for points on the Canadian National lines and which did not reach them. That has been a source of tribulation to the management of the Canadian National Railways for years past, and during certain seasons of the year the trouble has been very much accentuated. Of course, this is immensely more important to the shippers than it is even to the management of the railway, although they have to be the buffer between the two.
I regret very much that the original project has been abandoned. Perhaps, I can supply to the minister the reason, and I think the reason was this, that in the early days of this project and prior to last year, it was proposed to have this independent connection with New England, not with the existing railways in the Maine territory, but with a proposed new railway which would be built from the Maine boundary west to some New England point, such as Bangor. That project, I understand, unfortunately has fallen through. The promoters of that railway are not able to get their charter renewed. They have been delayed because of the delay on this side of the boundary, and within twelve months they have been denied a renewal of the franchise which they had heretofore. I think it is an unfortunate thing, from the standpoints of economy and of expenditure, that that should have occurred, and I imagine the officials of the Canadian National Railway system have been confronted with a new situation. I hope this matter will be approached from the standpoint of pure business, and if the line is not built this year, I venture to prophesy that it will be built within the near future unless some equitable arrangement can be made with the Canadian Pacific Railway.
While I am on my feet, let me say that we might as well be honest about the matter
and admit that from the standpoint of business, the weakness of the proposition is that, to a certain extent at all events, it is a duplication. But I sympathize from the bot-ton of my heart with the management of the Canadian National Railways, because of the difficulties which they have encountered on account of a line already existing which, in part at all events, gets this traffic. I cannot say anything more than I have said at this stage unless I know something more from the minister as to the routing and probable cost. I doubt very much if this road, from what I know of the first twelve miles at any rate, from St. John river south where it has to climb a very heavy watershed, can be built for $51,SOO a mile. I have not very much faith in the government railways being able to build economically, especially after the experience we had in New Brunswick with the Transcontinental railway before the war, that railway having cost, I am informed, as much as $110,000 a mile. However, I hope that the present management will not be quite as prodigal as the commissioners of the Transcontinental railway were in New Brunswick during the years from 1904 to 1910. In any case, 1 doubt very much whether the line can be built for the figure named in the resolution.
I want to point out to the minister that there are no expensive bridges to be considered, unless he duplicates or parallels that portion of the Canadian Pacific Railway line between Harvey and Vanceboro. If he does so he will find at least two very expensive bridges to build which will add materially to the cost.
I have endeavoured to be as sympathetic as possible to this proposition, but I should like to know whether it is really the intention of the management to begin operations this year. I can hardly believe it is, and I will tell the minister why, in advance. Up to last night the preliminary survey had not reached McAdam. I came by there last night and I knew that the engineers had been out for several weeks; but I was informed that the preliminary survey was still seven miles short of the westerly terminus, and it occurred to me that if the management were really serious in the intention to go on this year they had delayed that survey altogether too long. It is only fair to say, however, that the men are on the ground and are working towards their objective. I have no doubt, from the nature of the country, that the preliminary survey
C.N.R.-Branch Lines

can be put through in the course of a week at most, by which time it might be hoped that the bill would go through. Once again, I would ask the minister whether it is the bona fide intention of the management to start this line this year, provided of course the bill goes through.

I was very glad to hear the statement made by the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) that this project is a purely business proposition. I am sure that if the committee were familiar with the geographical position of the Maritime provinces and the railway situation in relation to the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific systems as it affects our trade with the United States, they would agree with my hon. friend that this branch line is not only sound from the business
standpoint, but is absolutely essential if Sir Henry Thornton is to operate the Canadian National railway in the Maritime provinces with any degree of success.
In the province of New Brunswick we have the Canadian National railway skirting the eastern shores of the province and continuing through my own province, being the only avenue by which Nova Scotia has connection with the transportation systems of the country. There is another line of the Canadian National running from Moncton westerly to St. John. Then another line starting from Newcastle runs to the city of Fredericton, whence my hon. friend from York-Sunbury comes.	But the freight of eastern New
Brunswick and of the whole province of Nova Scotia which is carried by rail to the United States is tributary to the Canadian Pacific railway.	It is all turned over
by the Canadian National to the Canadian Pacific at St. John or at Fredericton Junction, and all the efforts on the part of the managers of the Canadian National S3rs-tem to build up their freight business simply enure to the benefit of the Canadian Pacific railway. One can readily see the handicap that is being placed upon the fishermen, lumbermen and farmers of the Maritime provinces through having to pay freight charges not only to the Canadian National but also to the Canadian Pacific and the Boston and Maine.

Yes, where connections would be made, say at Fredericton Junction. As my hon. friend from Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud) has well said, the fishing products of the Maritime provinces find their principal market in Boston, both winter and summer, that being the great fish distributing centre of the United States. Then again, owing to the building boom in eastern United States during the past two years, the main market for all our lumber has been there; and so in regard to all our other products.
Now, the proposition which is recommended by the management of the Canadian National system is to build the line mentioned in the resolution so that they will have an independent entrance to the United States in connection with the Boston and Maine at

Vanceboro, and so cease being tributary to the Canadian Pacific railway with respect to freight originating on the National lines. To my mind there can be no question about the correctness of the statement made by my hon. friend from York-Sunbury that this is a business proposition. I am sure that my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. MacLaren), or rather his newspaper, is taking entirely too local a view of the situation, for I am sure that the great mass of the people in New Brunswick realize the facts to be as I have stated them, and I am confident they will say that if Sir Henry Thornton is to be held responsible for the successful management of the Canadian National railway system, he cannot, so far as our part of the country at least is concerned, be expected to continue to hand over all his traffic to an intermediate road and his greatest competitor.

subtopic: BILLS PROPOSED TO AUTHORIZE THE CONSTRUCTION OF BRANCH LINES
speechtext: I do not think this proposed branch line is as necessary as the arguments advanced by the last two speakers would seem to indicate. We already have outlets for New Brunswick and Maritime province products to the New England states. There is the Canadian Pacific from St. John to Vanceboro, also the lines along the St. John river to Fredericton and Woodstock and between Woodstock and McAdam junction. The project under consideration might be a fairly good proposition if economic conditions would warrant it, but in view of the present circumstances are we justified in making an initial expenditure of 82,123,000 for the construction of a small branch line between Kingsclear and a point on the St. Croix river opposite Vanceboro? If you do construct from Kingsclear to Vanceboro you cannot handle what traffic may come from the other parts of the Maritime provinces, with the exception of the northern section of New Brunswick.

speechtext: What is to prevent the traffic that centres at Moncton going over the Transcontinental to Fredericton and from there down?

subtopic: BILLS PROPOSED TO AUTHORIZE THE CONSTRUCTION OF BRANCH LINES
speechtext:
That could be done, Mr. Chairman, but it would be going somewhat out of the ordinary route, because the Transcontinental between St. John and Moncton and Fredericton has not been made much use of. But there are many sections of New Brunswick which need railway facilities much more than the part of the country dealt with in this resolution. For instance, we have a section in the northern part of the province to which reference has been made on various occasions in this House. Referring last year

to the question of acquiring the Kent Northern railway, the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) said:
As to the county of Kent, New Brunswick, the Kent Northern railway is twenty-seven miles long, and I quite appreciate the fact that it might just as well have been twenty-seven inches long so far as its operation has been of any practical value. The question has been discussed as to how these people can best be served in that section of the. country, because they are not served now. An effort was made by the previous government to take over the Kent Northern, and large petitions have come in from the county of Kent asking that the Moncton-Buctouche line be extended 18 miles to serve a greater number of people outside of the town of Richibucto, or Rexton, I believe, through which it passes. These matters are under consideration, and I have asked the management of the Canadian National Railways, as soon as they can possibly do so, to make a thorough investigation of the situation in the county of Kent, because my hon. friend behind me (Mr. Leger) has made my life miserable for the past three months over the question and will continue to do so, I am afraid, if I do not do something.
That road was built forty-one years ago and during the last few years it has been in the hands of a trust company. This company does not appear to be anxious to make any great capital expenditure. Last year the road was closed down for practically two months and this year it has again been unable to give the required service. I speak on behalf of the country immediately served by that road, representing the large and flourishing parishes of Richibucto, Welsford, St. Louis, St. Ignace, St. Charles and Carleton, with a total population of about 12,000. The conditions which induced my predecessor to impress upon the Minister of Railways the importance of doing something in this connection still exist, and I submit that before spending over two millions of the public money for the building of branch lines in a part of the province which is already well provided with railway facilities it would be much more advisable and much more in keeping with the giving of equal rights to all that something should be done in the matter of that branch line of 27 miles from Kent junction into Richibucto. It is true that some steps have been taken toward getting a line from Buctouche into Richibucto, a distance of 18 miles. Survey parties have been over that route and as a matter of fact that branch railway was promised no later than last December. Be that as it may, I do not intend to insist that that branch line be built if present conditions do not warrant it, but I do insist that on account of the Kent Northern railway from Kent Junc-9 p.m. tion into Richibucto being one of the only two independent branch lines in the Maritime provinces not taken over and made part of the National Railways in 1919, steps should be taken to acquire that

C.N.R.-Branch Lines
road either by purchase or by lease, with a view to giving service to the public. The people in that part of the country have been told that economy would have to be practised in connection with the railways. For twenty-eight years the people along the line of the Moncton and Buctouche railway, a distance of 32 miles, had a daily mail service, but since the first of January of this year the Wednesday trip has been cancelled so that to-day there is no connection between Moncton and Buctouche on Wednesday of each week, and therefore no mail distributed on that day. That condition did not prevail in the past except in cases of very stormy weather. The people in that section are entitled to better service. I submit that the vote placed in the estimates in 1919 and again passed as a revote in 1920, but which was unfortunately dropped because the company would not accept the offer made by the government at that time, should again be placed in the estimates this year with a view of acquiring the Kent Northern railway and improving the service in that part of the country, the people of which have been denied their just rights, as was represented to the committee a moment ago by the member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud), and also to provide a daily service on the Moncton and Buctouche branch line. And further more we are willing to practise economy, if that is necessary, but it is a very poor consolation to the people in that section of the country to hear so much about economy and then to see branch lines built in sections where those branches will parallel or duplicate existing lines.
